parts.title: More tree species and more genetic variety help trees grow, by giving them a wider range of leaf features and by changing how they interact with the living things around them
parts.abstract:
Around the world, many kinds of living things are disappearing. To tackle this, we need to pay attention to more than one side of biodiversity, the variety of life. Most studies have looked at what happens when a place has more or fewer plant species. We still know little about how genetic variety within a single plant species affects how much plants grow.

In this study, we used an experiment in which we changed both the number of tree species and the number of seed families of each species. A seed family is the group of young trees whose seeds came from the same mother tree, so they are closely related. This let us separate the effects of species variety from the effects of genetic variety on how much the trees grew. We also looked at how both were linked to two other things. The first was functional variety: how different the trees were in their leaf features. The second was trophic feedbacks: the ways plants are affected by the animals and other living things that feed on them.

We found that having more tree species helped the trees grow. It did this by increasing functional variety, by reducing the variety of fungi in the soil, and, to a smaller degree, by reducing leaf damage from plant-eating animals. Genetic variety had different effects in the two situations we compared. When each plot held only one species, genetic variety reduced growth through functional variety and soil fungi. In the mixture of the four tree species we tested, it increased growth through them.

The links between species variety, genetic variety, functional variety and trophic feedbacks are complicated. For this reason, we suggest that people who plant new forests should consider both the number of tree species and the genetic variety of those trees.
parts.introduction_first:
Biodiversity, the variety of life, is essential for keeping ecosystems working. It also matters for the many ways nature helps people, such as providing food, clean water and wood (Cardinale et al., 2012; Diaz et al., 2019). The world is losing biodiversity, and this has worried many countries and organizations (Ceballos et al., 2015). If we study more than one side of biodiversity, we can better predict what losing it will do. We can also decide which sides to protect first (Cardinale et al., 2012).

Many studies have asked how the number of species in a place affects important natural processes, such as how much plants grow. Scientists call this link between biodiversity and how ecosystems work the biodiversity–ecosystem functioning link (Hector et al., 1999; Huang et al., 2018; Tilman et al., 2001). Far fewer studies have asked what happens when there is more or less variety within a single species, for example more or less genetic variety.

The results for variety within a species are also mixed. In communities of non-woody plants, such as grasses and wildflowers, genetic variety has helped the plants grow more (Crutsinger et al., 2006; Kotowska et al., 2010). In forests, however, it has not (Bongers et al., 2020; Fischer et al., 2017). We want to understand how genetic variety affects the growth of trees in forests, so that we can help guide where and how to plant new forests. To do that, we need to work out the processes behind these effects.
parts.introduction_rest:
Functional variety is expected to help a plant community grow more. Different species, or different genetic types within a species, may use resources such as light, water and nutrients in ways that fit together. For example, one may use the light that another cannot reach. Together, they can then use more of the resources available to the whole community (Diaz and Cabido, 2001; Figure 1a). Scientists usually measure functional variety as how much the average leaf features of the species in a plant community differ from one another. Researchers have used it to explain how the number of plant species affects how much plants grow (Cadotte et al., 2011; Diaz et al., 2007; Hillebrand and Matthiessen, 2009).

Genetic variety is known to cause large differences in leaf features within a single species (Bongers et al., 2020). These differences within a species may also strongly affect how much plants grow (Des Roches et al., 2018; Koricheva et al., 2018). Even so, we still do not know how much genetic variety can affect tree growth by increasing functional variety.

Trophic feedbacks have been suggested as another way that biodiversity can help plants grow (Laforest-Lapointe et al., 2017). They come from the ways plants of different species or genetic types interact with other groups of living things, such as plant-eating animals and soil fungi. Trophic feedbacks can help a mixture of species or genetic types in two ways. First, they can reduce damage from plant-eating animals. This can happen when the plants differ more in the nutrients they contain (Wetzel et al., 2016) or in the chemicals they make (Bustos-Segura et al., 2017). Second, they can increase the variety of helpful partners, such as mycorrhizal fungi, which live on plant roots and help the plant take up water and nutrients (Semchenko et al., 2018; Figure 1b).

Functional variety can affect these trophic feedbacks (Schuldt et al., 2019). So can other things, such as structural variety, meaning how much the plants differ in their size and shape (Schuldt et al., 2019). These differences may give other groups of living things more chances to find a place to live and feed. Many studies have looked at how plant variety affects other groups of living things (Scherber et al., 2010; Schuldt et al., 2019). Others have looked at how these interactions affect how well plants grow (Eisenhauer, 2012; Semchenko et al., 2018). But few studies have looked at both together: how plant variety affects other groups of living things, and how those effects then feed back on plant growth.

In real ecosystems, we can hardly expect the number of plant species and genetic variety to act separately (Vellend and Geber, 2005). Earlier studies of communities of non-woody plants showed that more genetic variety can weaken competition between species. This changes the link between the number of plant species and how much plants grow (Schöb et al., 2015). In the same way, Siefert et al. (2015) showed that when there are more species, the differences in leaf features within a species become smaller compared with the differences between species. This is partly because of genetic variety.

Only a few forest experiments have changed both the number of species and the genetic variety at the same time. Most of them simply compared how much each one mattered for how the ecosystem worked (Abdala‐Roberts et al., 2015; Koricheva et al., 2018). We know very little about how the two work together to affect plant growth, through functional variety and trophic feedbacks.

In this study, we separate out how the number of tree species and genetic variety affect how much trees grow, by looking at their effects on functional variety and trophic feedbacks. We used data from a long-running experiment in a subtropical forest, where we changed both the number of tree species and the genetic variety (Bruelheide et al., 2014; Biodiversity–Ecosystem Functioning Experiment China Platform [BEF-China], https://www.bef-china.com). Each plot held either one or four tree species. Within each species, each plot held either one or four seed families. We combined these choices in every possible way, which gave four levels of plant variety (Figure 1c).

We measured five leaf features, both their shape and their chemistry. Earlier work has shown that these features are linked to how plants take up resources (Cornelissen et al., 2003), and that they can vary a lot both between species and within a species (Albert et al., 2010). We measured functional variety as how much these five features differed among the seed families (Laliberté and Legendre, 2010).

We measured trophic interactions in two ways. For plant-eating animals, we measured them directly, by recording leaf damage. For soil fungi, we used the variety of fungi as a stand-in. This captures general interactions that may help explain the biodiversity–ecosystem functioning link (Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2016).

In particular, we tested whether having more tree species and more genetic variety helped the trees grow by increasing functional variety (Figure 1a) and through trophic feedbacks (Figure 1b). We also tested whether genetic variety mattered more when each plot held only one species than when it held a mixture of species. In a mixture, genetic variety between species may make up for the lack of genetic variety within each species (Figure 1c).
parts.methods:
## Materials and methods

### Where we worked and how we set up the experiment

We carried out this study in the species × genetic variety experiment of BEF-China (https://www.bef-china.com; Bruelheide et al., 2014; Hahn et al., 2017). BEF-China is a large experiment in which scientists test how the variety of life affects how forests work. It lies close to Xingangshan, in Dexing City, Jiangxi Province, China. The average temperature over the year is 16.7 °C, and on average 1821 mm of rain and snow falls each year.

The experiment was set up in 2010. It has 24 plots, each 25.8 × 25.8 m, which is one Chinese unit of land called a 'mu'. Each plot was planted with 400 young trees chosen from a pool of four species: Alniphyllum fortunei, Cinnamomum camphora, Daphniphyllum oldhamii and Idesia polycarpa. We know the mother tree of every one of these trees (Appendix 1—figure 1). We call the young trees from the same mother tree a seed family. We assumed that trees from different seed families differ more in their genes than trees from the same seed family (Bongers et al., 2020; Hahn et al., 2017). The young trees of one mother tree could have had different fathers, so each seed family was somewhere between a full-sib family (all brothers and sisters) and a half-sib family (half brothers and sisters). For this reason, we used the number of seed families of each species as our measure of genetic variety (Bruelheide et al., 2014).

Across the 24 plots, we combined species variety (one or four species) with genetic variety (one or four seed families per species). This gave four levels of tree variety: one species with one seed family (1.1), one species with four seed families (1.4), four species with one seed family each (4.1), and four species with four seed families each (4.4) (Appendix 1—figure 1; Bongers et al., 2020).

For each of the four species, we collected seeds from eight mother trees. This gave us two repeats of the four-family mixtures for each species. We also wanted to avoid two problems. One was that some seed families might be more common than others. The other was that which seed families were present might be linked to the variety level. To avoid both, we made sure that every seed family appeared the same number of times at each variety level (see Appendix 1—table 1). In a few cases we could not get enough seeds from a seed family, so we had to make small exceptions to this rule.

Our budget was limited, and we needed several repeats of each seed family. So we planted the 1.1 and 1.4 levels in smaller areas called subplots, each one quarter of a mu (0.25 mu). We had 32 subplots of 1.1 and 8 subplots of 1.4. We planted the 4.1 and 4.4 levels in whole plots (1 mu), with eight subplots of 4.1 and six subplots of 4.4 (Appendix 1—figure 1; see also Figure 1 in Bongers et al., 2020).

To make the analysis simpler, we measured most of our forest features at the subplot level, even in the 4.1 and 4.4 plots. We then used the subplots for all our tests of how variety affected these features. In these tests we used a mixed model (explained below), which took into account that subplots in the same plot tend to be alike. In statistics this is called a random effect, and here it was the plot. In total, we used 92 subplots: 32 of 1.1, 8 of 1.4, 28 of 4.1 and 24 of 4.4. We could not set up one whole 1-mu plot of each level because of practical limits. In biodiversity experiments, the levels with fewer species each stand for many different communities, so they need more plots. The level with the most species usually has only one possible mix of species, so the same community is repeated many times, as we did for the 4.4 level.

### Tree leaf features and functional variety

In 2017 and 2018 we measured five leaf features: leaf area (LA), specific leaf area (SLA, how much leaf area a tree gets from each gram of leaf), chlorophyll content (CHL, the green pigment that captures sunlight), leaf nitrogen content (LN) and leaf carbon content (LC). These features can show how well a plant gathers the resources it needs, such as light, water and nutrients. They can vary a lot, not only between species but also within a species (Albert et al., 2010; Cornelissen et al., 2003). We measured them on 547 trees, covering all the seed families of the four species at every combination of species and genetic variety (Appendix 1—table 2). Bongers et al. (2020) describe the details.

We measured functional variety as functional dispersion (FDis). This is the average distance of each seed family from the centre point of all the seed families in the community (Laliberté and Legendre, 2010). In other words, it tells us how spread out the seed families are in their leaf features.

We wanted to avoid a circular problem. If we used the leaf features measured in a subplot to calculate functional variety for that same subplot, the features might simply be a response to the local conditions there. We then wanted to use functional variety to predict how well that subplot grew. To avoid this, we calculated functional variety for each subplot from the average leaf features of each seed family across all the variety levels. This way, the values did not depend on the measurements from that one subplot. In every mixture, each seed family and each species counted equally, because we planted equal numbers of them in each subplot.

A few subplots had seed families with no leaf measurements. We filled in their values with the average functional variety for that species and genetic variety level (Appendix 1—table 2).

We also calculated another common measure of functional variety, Rao's Q (Rao, 1982). However, Rao's Q and functional dispersion were strongly linked: they rose and fell together. This was true in simulated data (Laliberté and Legendre, 2010) and in our study (Appendix 2—figure 2). When each seed family counts equally, functional dispersion should also work better than Rao's Q (Laliberté and Legendre, 2010). So we used only functional dispersion in the analyses in this paper. We calculated both measures with the 'dbFD' function of the 'FD' package (version 1.0–12.1) in R, a free program for statistics (Laliberté et al., 2014, https://www.r-project.org).

We also calculated functional dispersion from the leaf features of individual trees, across all the variety levels. This version had one advantage. It could also be calculated for subplots planted with trees from a single seed family. With the seed-family averages, such subplots had a value of zero, but this version showed the functional variety within a seed family. It had one disadvantage, though. It probably included more variation caused by the surroundings, because each tree responds to many unknown factors in its local environment.

We also calculated community-weighted means (CWMs) for the five leaf features. A community-weighted mean is the average of a feature across all the trees in a community, with common species counting more than rare ones. To combine the five features into a few summary scores, we used a method called principal component analysis (PCA). PCA finds the main patterns in a set of measurements. We used a version called varimax rotation, which makes each pattern as easy to interpret as possible. This gave us two separate summary scores, called principal components. Together they captured 64% of the variation in the leaf features (Appendix 2—table 2). The first score (PC1) reflected the leaf features directly linked to growth, and the second (PC2) reflected the features linked to photosynthesis, the way plants use sunlight to make food (Appendix 2—figure 3). We ran this analysis with the 'psych' package for R, version 2.1.9 (Makowski, 2018).

### How trees interact with other living things

#### Leaf damage from plant-eating animals

Leaf damage from plant-eating animals comes from the contact between plants and the animals that eat them, and it can be recorded as damage to leaves. In 2017, for every tree, we picked four or five damaged leaves at random and estimated by eye how much of each leaf had been eaten (Johnson et al., 2016). These were the same 547 trees we used for the leaf features (see above). In this study, leaf damage is the percentage of each damaged leaf that plant-eating animals had eaten. We counted together the damage caused by chewers, gall formers (insects that make swellings on the plant), leaf miners (insects that tunnel inside leaves) and leaf rollers (insects that roll leaves into tubes).

Because we only collected damaged leaves, we might have overestimated the leaf damage for each tree. To correct for this, we used data from other plots of the BEF-China experiment (Schuldt et al., 2015), which did not leave out undamaged leaves. That earlier study looked at 21 leaves (7 leaves per branch) on three branches picked at random from different parts of the tree's crown (Schuldt et al., 2015). It used the average percentage damage as the total leaf damage for each tree.

For all four species, we then compared the total leaf damage from that study with the damage per damaged leaf, using linear regression. Linear regression finds the straight line that best describes how one measurement changes with another. The two measures were very closely linked (Pearson's correlation = 0.86–0.96, p < 0.001) (Appendix 2—table 3). Pearson's correlation runs from −1 to 1, and values near 1 mean two measures rise together very closely. The p-value tells us that if there were really no link, a link this strong would turn up by chance less than 0.1% of the time.

We used these regression lines to predict leaf damage for our study, and we used these predictions in our final analyses. A few subplots had trees with no leaf damage data. We filled in their values with the average leaf damage for that species and genetic variety level (Appendix 1—table 2).

#### Variety of fungi in the soil

We used the variety of fungi in the soil as a stand-in for trophic feedbacks that we could not measure directly. To match the way we set up the species and genetic variety levels, we took soil samples at the subplot level for the 1.1 and 1.4 levels. For the 4.1 and 4.4 levels, we could only take them at the plot level in 2017. In each subplot or plot, we collected five soil samples from the top 0–5 cm of soil, at the four corners and the centre. We then mixed the five samples together.

We packed each soil sample with dry ice and took it to the laboratory, where we stored it at −80°C until we extracted its DNA. We extracted the total DNA from a small portion of each sample using a Soil Genomic DNA Kit (Tiangen Biotech Co., Beijing, China), following the maker's instructions. We then used PCR, a method that makes many copies of one chosen stretch of DNA. We copied a stretch called the internal transcribed spacer 2 (ITS2) from the DNA in the cell nucleus. To do this, we used two primers, short pieces of DNA that mark where copying starts and stops: ITS3F (GCATCGATGAAGAACGCAGC) and ITS4R (TCCTCCGCTTATTGATATGC).

We processed the DNA sequences with the QIIME 2 software (https://docs.qiime2.org/). This grouped the sequences into operational taxonomic units (OTUs), groups of sequences that are treated as one kind of fungus. Some samples had been read more deeply than others, meaning more sequences were recorded for them. To make them fair to compare, we randomly cut every sample down to the same number of sequences, 10,975. We then named the fungi using the UNITE database (Nilsson et al., 2019).

From the names and numbers of fungi in each subplot or plot, we calculated the Chao1 index (Chao, 1984). This index estimates the total number of kinds of fungi, including rare ones that may have been missed. We chose it because most fungal species in our study were fairly rare, and Chao1 handles rare species well (Chao, 1984). We calculated it with the 'vegan' package for R, version 2.5–7 (Oksanen et al., 2019).

#### How much the trees grew

In 2018 we measured the height (H) of every tree in the plots and its basal area (BA), the area of a slice across the trunk (Bongers et al., 2020). We calculated the biomass of each tree, its weight in kilograms, with the BEF-China biomass equation (H × BA × CV) (Huang et al., 2018). Here CV is a correction factor that takes into account the shape of the trunk and how dense the wood is. Huang et al. (2018) give more details about the equation. We added up the biomass of all the trees in a subplot to get tree community productivity, the amount of tree growth, in tonnes per hectare (Mg ha–1).

### How we analysed the data

First, we looked at how tree variety, trophic feedbacks and tree growth were linked to each other. To find out how species variety, genetic variety and the way they act together affected functional variety and trophic feedbacks, we used linear mixed-effects models (LMMs). These are statistical models that test how several factors affect an outcome while taking into account that some measurements are grouped together. We fitted them in two ways of setting up the factors, called contrast coding.

In the first way, we used the ordinary two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with an interaction. An ANOVA tests whether the average of an outcome differs between groups. An interaction means that the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other. In the second way, we replaced the overall effect of genetic variety, and the interaction, with separate effects of genetic variety for the single-species plots and for the mixture of species (Appendix 2—table 4). Because our design was balanced, the order in which we fitted the factors did not matter in either way. However, we focused our main analysis on the second way, because it matched our hypotheses. The overall effects of genetic variety are shown in the small panels in Figure 2. The second way let us test the effects of genetic variety separately in the single-species plots and in the mixture, but within the same analysis.

In all the mixed models, we included 'plot' as a random effect, because subplots were grouped inside plots. This also made sure that factors whose levels did not change from subplot to subplot within a plot (specifically, the four-species variety levels) were tested against the differences between plots, rather than against the leftover differences between subplots. We fitted the mixed models in R with the 'lmer' function of the lme4 package, version 1.1.27.1 (Bates et al., 2015). We used the lmerTest package, version 3.1.3 (Kuznetsova et al., 2017), to calculate the F-statistics and the Kenward–Roger's method for the degrees of freedom. These are the numbers used to judge whether an effect is larger than chance alone would usually produce.

To meet the assumptions of the mixed models, we transformed the proportion of leaf damage caused by plant-eating animals with an angular transformation (Snedecor and Cochran, 1989). This is a standard way of rescaling proportions so that they suit the model. To draw the regression lines in Figure 3, we used linear models ('lm' function in R) that linked tree community productivity to functional variety, leaf damage from plant-eating animals and the variety of fungi in the soil, for the four variety levels.

Second, we fitted structural equation models (SEMs). These test a whole network of cause-and-effect paths at once, and we showed the results as path diagrams (Grace, 2006). We used the 'piecewiseSEM' package for R, version 2.1.2 (Lefcheck, 2016). We used them to test our ideas about how the effects of tree species and genetic variety on tree growth could have passed through functional variety and trophic feedbacks. We built the starting model from the most relevant paths based on theory (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). We also used separate linear regressions to check the links between the variables that we thought were related in the SEMs.

We assumed that both genetic variety and species variety could affect trophic feedbacks and tree growth directly, or indirectly, by working through functional variety (Müller et al., 2018; Scherber et al., 2010; Schuldt et al., 2019). We also assumed that functional variety, leaf damage from plant-eating animals and the variety of fungi in the soil all had direct feedbacks on tree growth (Eisenhauer, 2012; Semchenko et al., 2018). We then removed paths that did not add information, one at a time, if removing a path lowered the AICc of the SEM by more than 2 (Grace, 2006). AICc is a score that rewards a model for fitting the data well but penalises it for being too complicated, and a lower score is better. The link between genetic variety and functional variety, calculated from seed-family averages, might distort the results. To check for this, we also fitted an SEM without the path between genetic variety and functional variety.

Third, we fitted separate SEMs for the single-species plots and for the mixtures. We did this because the ANOVAs showed statistically significant interactions between species and genetic variety, which meant that genetic variety had different effects in the single-species plots and in the mixtures. The starting path diagram for these models is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2. We simplified it in the same way as above, by comparing AICc values. For these models, we also fitted one more version without the path between genetic variety and functional variety.

Finally, to check how solid our results were, we repeated the analyses with the same paths as in the final single-path and multi-path models, but this time using functional dispersion calculated from the leaf features of individual trees. We carried out all the analyses in R 4.0.5.
parts.results:
## Results

### How tree variety, trophic feedbacks and tree growth were linked, two at a time

We first looked at how each pair of things was linked, two at a time. We used linear mixed models, a kind of statistical model that can compare groups while allowing for the fact that some measurements are grouped together. With these models, we tested how species variety and genetic variety affected trophic feedbacks and how much the trees grew.

Overall, the trees grew more in the mixture of four species than in the plots where each of the four species grew alone (Figure 2a). This difference was statistically significant. We call a result statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. Genetic variety, on the other hand, had no main effect on how much the trees grew in these two-at-a-time analyses (Figure 2a).

Functional variety was higher in the mixture than in the plots with one species. It was also higher in genetic mixtures than in genetic monocultures (Figure 2b). A genetic monoculture is a plot with one species and only one seed family of it.

The effects of genetic variety on functional variety, leaf damage from plant-eating animals and the variety of fungi in the soil were different in plots with one species than in the mixture. In plots with one species, functional variety was larger when there were four seed families than when there was one. In the mixture, however, it did not differ between plots with four seed families and plots with one (Figure 2b).

We also worked out functional variety in a second way, using measurements taken on each single tree rather than averages for each seed family. This time, only species variety, and not genetic variety, affected functional variety (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This suggests that differences within each seed family were hiding some of the differences between seed families.

Leaf damage and the variety of soil fungi were similar in plots with one species, whether that species had one or four seed families. In the mixture, both were lower in plots with four seed families than in plots with one (Figure 2c and d). Every treatment had the same number of seed families (Appendix 1—table 1). For this reason, we found no statistically significant effects of species variety or genetic variety on the community-weighted means of the tree features (Appendix 2—table 1). A community-weighted mean is an average of a feature across all the trees in a plot, in which each tree counts according to how much it contributes to the plot.

**Figure 2.** How much the trees grew, their functional variety and their trophic feedbacks in plots with low and high species variety and genetic variety.

We tested these effects with linear mixed models (92 plots). In each panel, the left and right bars show the main effect of species variety, and the small inset at the upper left shows the main effect of genetic variety. The arrows between the bars in each pair show the effect of genetic variety within each level of species variety. (a) How much the trees grew. (b) Functional variety. (c) Leaf damage from plant-eating animals. (d) Variety of fungi in the soil. Each bar shows the middle half of the values, from the 25th to the 75th percentile. The whiskers reach 1.5 times the height of the bar beyond it. Asterisks show statistical significance (*** p < 0.0001, ** p < 0.001, * p < 0.05). A solid arrow means p < 0.05, and no arrow means p > 0.1. Details of the models are in Appendix 2—table 1.

**Figure 2—figure supplement 1.** How species variety and genetic variety affected functional variety, when functional variety was worked out from measurements on single trees.

Each bar shows the middle half of the values, from the 25th to the 75th percentile. The whiskers reach 1.5 times the height of the bar beyond it (92 plots). Asterisks show statistical significance (*** p < 0.0001, ** p < 0.001, * p < 0.05, + p < 0.1, and ns p > 0.1). Details of the models are in Appendix 2—table 1.

Whether we used seed-family averages or measurements on single trees, functional variety had a positive overall effect on how much the trees grew. This effect came mainly from functional variety being higher in the mixture than in the plots with one species (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Leaf damage and the variety of soil fungi both had negative overall effects on growth (Figure 3b and c). The effect of leaf damage was marginally significant, meaning p was below 0.1 but not below 0.05. The effect of soil fungi was statistically significant.

The effects of leaf damage were also different in genetic monocultures and genetic mixtures within the plots with one species (Figure 3b). The effects of soil fungi were different in genetic monocultures and genetic mixtures within the mixture (Figure 3c).

**Figure 3.** How the amount the trees grew was linked to functional variety (a), leaf damage from plant-eating animals (b) and the variety of fungi in the soil (c).

The symbols show four kinds of plot. Green open or dashed symbols are genetic monocultures in plots with one species. Green filled or solid symbols are genetic monocultures in the mixture. Orange open or dashed symbols are genetic mixtures in plots with one species. Orange filled or solid symbols are genetic mixtures in the mixture. FDis, functional variety; Herb, leaf damage; Fungal, variety of soil fungi; Sp-mono, plots with one species; Sp-mix, the mixture; SD, species variety; GD, genetic variety. A colon (:) marks an interaction, where the effect of one thing depends on another. Asterisks show statistical significance (*** p < 0.0001, ** p < 0.001, * p < 0.05, + p < 0.1, and ns p > 0.1).

**Figure 3—figure supplement 1.** How functional variety, worked out from measurements on single trees, affected how much the trees grew.

Asterisks show statistical significance (*** p < 0.0001, ** p < 0.001, * p < 0.05, + p < 0.1, and ns p > 0.1). Details of the models are in Appendix 2—table 1.

### How functional variety and trophic feedbacks explain the effects of species variety and genetic variety on tree growth

To explain how species variety and genetic variety affected growth and trophic feedbacks, we used a structural equation model. This is a diagram of arrows, called paths, that links several measurements to each other. It lets us see both direct effects and indirect effects that pass through other measurements.

Species variety and genetic variety helped the trees grow, and they changed trophic feedbacks, mainly indirectly through functional variety (Figure 4). Functional variety rose much more as species variety increased than as genetic variety increased. We measured the strength of each path with a standardized path coefficient, a number that puts all paths on the same scale so they can be compared. The coefficient was 0.960 for species variety and only 0.074 for genetic variety (Figure 4). Leaf damage and the variety of soil fungi both reduced how much the trees grew (Figure 4, see also Figure 3b and c).

Overall, species variety and genetic variety affected growth in opposite ways through different routes. Both increased functional variety. Functional variety then increased growth directly, but it also reduced growth indirectly, through the harmful effects of leaf damage and soil fungi. At the same time, species variety and genetic variety also helped growth indirectly by reducing the variety of soil fungi. Genetic variety also helped through reduced leaf damage (Figure 4).

Functional variety and trophic feedbacks explained all the effects of species variety on growth. For genetic variety, however, a direct negative effect on growth was left over that our measured factors could not explain (Figure 4).

We also ran the analysis with functional variety worked out from measurements on single trees. It showed that species variety and genetic variety affected growth through functional variety and trophic feedbacks, although the effects of functional variety were weaker (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This may be because functional variety from single trees included more response functional variety (Sapijanskas et al., 2014) than functional variety from seed-family averages. Response functional variety is the part of the differences between trees that comes from how each tree responds to its surroundings. In addition, when we removed the path from genetic variety to functional variety, the other results we found with seed-family averages did not change (Figure 4, Appendix 3—figure 1).

**Figure 4.** How tree variety affected trophic feedbacks and how much the trees grew.

The whole model fitted the data well (global Fisher's C = 1.677, DF = 4, p = 0.795). Green arrows show positive paths and orange arrows show negative paths. The numbers are standardized path coefficients, and asterisks show statistical significance (*** p < 0.0001, ** p < 0.001, * p < 0.05, and + p < 0.1). The percentages show how much of the variation in each measurement the model explains. The gray dashed line is a path that was not statistically significant (p > 0.1) in the final model. We removed the direct path from species variety to growth because it was not statistically significant (p > 0.5). Removing it also lowered the AICc, a score that rewards a model for fitting well while staying simple, by more than 2 (ΔAICc = 3.269).

The whole model did not fit the data as well (global Fisher's C = 119.558, DF = 4, p = 0.001). Green arrows show positive paths and orange arrows show negative paths. Functional variety (based on FDis) is the average distance of the seed-family averages from the center of all the seed families. Herbivory is the percentage of leaf damage from plant-eating animals. The variety of soil fungi was measured with the Chao1 index, a common way of estimating how many kinds of fungi are present. Community productivity is how much the trees grew in the subplots (Mg ha–1, tonnes per hectare).

### How genetic variety affected growth in plots with one species and in the mixture

We then ran the analysis separately for plots with one species and for the mixture (Figure 5). This went against what we had expected. In plots with one species, genetic variety reduced how much the trees grew, through functional variety and through the variety of soil fungi. In the mixture, it had positive effects through the variety of soil fungi (see also Figures 2b and 3a).

When we used functional variety from measurements on single trees, genetic variety had a weaker effect on functional variety (path coefficient = 0.193, compared with 0.883). Even so, the effect of genetic variety on growth through functional variety in plots with one species kept the same direction and stayed statistically significant. In the mixture, functional variety had a positive effect on growth when we used measurements on single trees, but this effect was not statistically significant when we used seed-family averages (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

Genetic variety also helped growth indirectly through leaf damage in both plots with one species and in the mixture. This came from two negative paths: one from genetic variety to leaf damage, and one from leaf damage to growth. Using functional variety from single trees did not change the effects of genetic variety through trophic feedbacks, except that the effect of leaf damage on growth went from marginally significant to not statistically significant.

When we left out the effects of genetic variety on functional variety in the analyses using seed-family averages, the other path coefficients did not change (Figure 5, Appendix 3—figure 2). In plots with one species, genetic variety reduced growth indirectly through functional variety, which is the opposite of what we found in the combined analysis. This negative effect was balanced out by a positive direct effect of genetic variety on growth. This shows that other things, beyond the five leaf features we measured, were important.

We used a multigroup structural equation model, which fits the same model to two groups at once (global Fisher's C = 3.416, DF = 4, p = 0.491). The multigroup analysis works in two steps. First, it uses the full dataset to test whether the effect of each factor differs between the two groups. Then, depending on whether that difference is statistically significant, it estimates the path coefficient for each path using either the full dataset or the data from one group (plots with one species, or the mixture). Because of this, we could not get the percentage of the variation explained in the local multigroup model. We allowed every path to differ between plots with one species and the mixture, and we did not fix any path to be the same in both groups beforehand. ## Discussion

Our study shows that changing both the number of tree species and the genetic variety, and changing them together, can reveal the effects of each one on how much the trees grow. It can also reveal their interaction, which is when the effect of one depends on the level of the other.

Our first hypothesis was that both kinds of variety would help the trees grow. As we predicted, we found that both species variety and genetic variety can increase how much the trees grow. They do this by increasing functional variety and by changing trophic feedbacks. This suggests two ways in which variety can help. Species variety may help because different species use resources in different ways, so together they use more of what is available. Genetic variety may help because different trees within a species fill different roles in the community.

However, the effects of genetic variety on growth through functional variety were weaker than the effects of species variety. The effects of genetic variety on trophic feedbacks, on the other hand, were strong (see Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This suggests that the processes behind the effects of genetic variety may partly differ from those behind the effects of species variety, as we discuss below.

Our second hypothesis was that genetic variety would help the trees grow through functional variety and soil fungi. This is what we found in the plots where each plot held only one species. In the mixture of the four tree species, however, genetic variety had the opposite effect. This did not match our predictions. Below, we discuss these results in more detail.

### Tree species variety and genetic variety affect tree growth mainly through functional variety and trophic feedbacks

We used structural equation models (SEMs). These are statistical tools that test a whole network of possible links at once, such as from species variety to functional variety, and from functional variety to growth. They are shown in the path diagrams in Figure 4. When we looked at each link on its own, only species variety, and not genetic variety, affected how much the trees grew. But in the full models, both kinds of variety increased tree growth and trophic feedbacks through functional variety.

Functional variety in the trees seemed to help the community as a whole use resources in ways that complement each other (Kahmen et al., 2006; Marquard et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2017). This, in turn, increased how much the trees grew. At the same time, functional variety also gave more opportunities to plant-eating animals that eat many kinds of plants, and to soil fungi. This reduced how much the trees grew. We found the same for these tree species in a field study nearby (Brezzi et al., 2017).

We expect plant-eating animals to reduce plant growth in two ways. They remove leaf area (Zvereva et al., 2012), and the leaves that remain carry out less photosynthesis, the process plants use to make food from sunlight (Nabity et al., 2009). They also reduce growth through trade-offs between growing and defending against plant-eating animals (Züst and Agrawal, 2017). The harmful effect of soil fungi on growth fits with the finding that most of these fungi were saprophytes, which feed on dead material (Appendix 2—figure 1). Saprophytic fungi compete with plants for resources (Kaye and Hart, 1997; van der Heijden et al., 2008). Indeed, a related study in the same region found that more variety of saprophytic fungi reduced how well the ecosystem carried out several natural processes at once (Schuldt et al., 2018).

After we took the links through functional variety into account, species variety and genetic variety still had indirect positive effects on growth. These came through less leaf damage from plant-eating animals and through fewer soil fungi, and they increased how much the trees grew (see Figure 4). This matches earlier findings that plant variety may weaken harmful feedbacks from other groups of living things. It does this by reducing how many specialist enemies there are, and how varied they are (e.g., Duffy, 2003; Jactel and Brockerhoff, 2007).

We also wanted to allow for the fact that trees from the same seed family may be alike. So we also calculated functional variety from the measurements of individual trees (see 'Materials and methods'). Overall, the results from this new method still support our hypotheses. Both tree species variety and genetic variety affect how much the trees grow through functional variety and through trophic feedbacks across several levels of the food web (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

The new method does include more of the differences between individual trees than the 'mean' method, which is the one usually used. Part of these differences reflect how each tree's features respond to its particular local surroundings (Sapijanskas et al., 2014). This may have blurred the average effects of genetic variety and species variety (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

At the same time, the results suggest that the seed-family mean method may create a false effect of genetic variety on functional variety. This happens because functional variety is zero in plots that hold only one species and one seed family (1.1 communities). However, when we left out the link between genetic variety and functional variety, the other links in the model did not change. This shows that the partly artificial link between genetic variety and functional variety did not distort the model as a whole (Figure 4, Appendix 3—figure 1).

Even after we took functional variety and trophic feedbacks into account, we still found a direct negative effect of genetic variety on tree growth. The direct effect of species variety, by contrast, was fully explained by functional variety and trophic feedbacks. This suggests that some parts of genetic variety may reduce how well the ecosystem works, even though they did not add to functional variety or trophic feedbacks in our study. One example is a trade-off between genetic variety and species variety.

For example, studies of grasslands with many species have shown that species can complement each other in using resources, but this can come at the cost of less variety within each species (van Moorsel et al., 2018; van Moorsel et al., 2019; Zuppinger-Dingley et al., 2014; Zvereva et al., 2012). So, in our experiment, the high genetic variety within species in the mixtures might have reduced the positive effects of having many species. This explanation would fit with what we saw in the separate path diagrams. There, genetic variety had direct negative effects on growth only in the mixtures, while in the plots with one species these effects were positive (see the next section). Whatever the explanation, our finding could also mean that species variety and genetic variety affect how ecosystems work partly through different processes (Barantal et al., 2019; Des Roches et al., 2018).

### The effects of genetic variety differ between plots with one species and mixtures

This did not match our second hypothesis. In the plots with one species, genetic variety reduced growth through functional variety and through soil fungi. In the mixture, the effects were not statistically significant through functional variety, and they were positive through soil fungi (Figure 5). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no effect, a result this large would rarely appear by chance alone. 'Not significant' means we could not show an effect, not that there is none.

In the plots with one species, genetic variety increased functional variety and soil fungi. In the mixture, it reduced them. This supports the trade-offs between genetic variety and species variety discussed in the previous section. However, the positive effect we expected from functional variety on growth turned negative in the plots with one species. This result suggests that functional variety may not help the ecosystem work when the surroundings are very uniform, as they were in our plots with one species (Hillebrand and Matthiessen, 2009).

Other parts of tree genetic variety also seem to play an important role. This is true not only for growth in mixtures (see the previous section) but also for growth in plots with one species. These may include features of the trees that we did not measure, such as root features (Bardgett et al., 2014). They may also include processes behind the effects of tree genetic variety that are still unknown.

We calculated functional variety in two ways: from the averages for each seed family, or from the features of individual trees. The two methods gave different results for the indirect effects of genetic variety on tree growth through functional variety. The seed-family method has the advantage of being less circular, because it does not use the same information twice. The method based on individual trees has the advantage of giving functional variety values above zero even in plots with one species and one seed family (1.1 communities; see 'Materials and methods').

With the individual-tree method, the indirect effects of genetic variety on growth through functional variety were weaker. This suggests that the zero value of functional variety in 1.1 communities, used in the seed-family method, may make these indirect effects look larger than they really are in plots with one species. Even so, the seed-family method is still useful for plots with one species that contain several seed families, and for mixtures.

## Conclusions

In this study, we tried to separate the effects of tree species variety and genetic variety on how much the trees grow. We looked at these effects through functional variety and trophic feedbacks, in a simple experiment with four species and several seed families of each. Setting up, managing and measuring this experiment, using trees and soil samples, was already challenging. Larger studies will be needed to show whether our results apply more widely.

Even so, our results suggest that both species variety and genetic variety played a part in affecting how much the trees grew. This was true both for how resources were shared out between species, and for how they were shared out between different genetic types within a species (Turnbull et al., 2016). Both kinds of variety contributed to growth, but the processes behind them differed, and the processes behind genetic variety were harder to explain. We suggest that trade-offs between tree species variety and genetic variety may cause the effect of genetic variety to change in strength and direction between plots with one species and mixtures.

We could not firmly show that trophic feedbacks cause changes in tree growth, because we did not experimentally change leaf damage from plant-eating animals or the soil fungi. However, our results do support the hypothesis that trophic feedbacks affect how much plant communities grow. Planting new forests is important for limiting carbon loss and for bringing ecological and economic benefits (Brockerhoff et al., 2008; Lamb et al., 2005). For this reason, we strongly recommend that both tree species variety and genetic variety should be considered when planting new forests.
